articles.description: The Network tab in browser DevTools tells you quite a bit about a request, including how long DNS resolution and the TLS handshake took. The time waiting for the server is less helpful. There is a bar labeled “Waiting for server response”, but no indication of whether the application was waiting for a database query or calling another API. With the Server-Timing response header, an application can include its own measurements. Chrome, Edge, and Firefox display these alongside the timings the browser already collects.
articles.title: Server-Timing Headers in ASP.NET Core: Backend Metrics in Browser DevTools

articles.description: A session cookie is a bearer token, which is a polite way of saying that whoever holds it is you. Copy the cookie, replay it from another machine, and the server happily serves your account. Nothing about the request proves which device it came from, so a cookie lifted by malware, an XSS payload, or a stray database backup keeps working until it expires. For a long-lived session, that can be weeks.
articles.title: Device Bound Session Credentials in ASP.NET Core

articles.description:
Anyone who has put a customer support agent backed by a large language model in front of real users has, sooner or later, watched it cheerfully write a Python web scraper or summarize last night’s football results, simply because somebody asked nicely. The usual remedy is to add a few more lines to the system prompt, asking the model to politely decline anything outside of its remit, however such approach means that every off-topic request still costs a full call to the support model, and that the very same model which is supposed to stay on topic is also the one deciding whether the request is on topic in the first place.
In this post we will look at a different arrangement, in which the scope decision is taken away from the support model altogether and handed over to Microsoft-Decision-1, a new model in Microsoft Foundry that does not generate any text at all, wired into a Microsoft Agent Framework agent as a piece of run middleware.
articles.title: Scope gating Agent Framework agents with Microsoft-Decision-1

articles.description:
Entanglement is fragile, and one of the more striking ways in which it is fragile was pointed out by Ting Yu and Joseph Eberly in 2004. Two qubits left to relax independently, each of them losing its excitation to its own environment, need not lose their entanglement gradually, the way the excitations themselves decay. Prepared in the state $\alpha|00\rangle + \beta|11\rangle$ with the doubly excited component the larger one, $|\beta| > |\alpha|$, they lose it completely at a finite time and it stays lost (for $|\beta| \leq |\alpha|$ it merely fades away), a phenomenon which Yu and Eberly named entanglement sudden death, and which was subsequently observed in a photonic experiment by Almeida and colleagues in 2007.
The reason it never comes back is, in fact, rather general. Once a state is…
articles.title: Sudden Death of Entanglement, Rebirth of Magic: Amplitude Damping in Q#
